title: The Marginal Yield of LLM-Guided Alpha Search: Search Effort, Information and Investment Value
abstract: Language models can propose stock-return factors without limit, so the useful question is what an additional proposal is worth to an investor. We follow the gain from continued search through three stages: the training score the search optimizes, the accuracy of a joint return forecast, and the net return of a long-only portfolio. Paired experiments vary the search policy, the information available to the search and the downstream learner. The gain is stage-dependent. Training scores improve quickly and then saturate; price-volume search raises its best score by 17% within twelve further proposals. Little of this carries through. Repairing diagnosed formula defects raises factor scores while lowering forecast accuracy, and no policy changes net return by an amount distinguishable from zero. Tracing the libraries through the pipeline shows where the gains thin out: new factors overlap more with features the model already uses than the factors they replace, re-estimation offsets part of their contribution, and the stocks they add earn about what the displaced stocks earned, so transaction costs are not the cause. Research effort on factor search is best judged by the return it delivers, not by the score it optimizes.
why: LLM alpha search shows net-return gains vanish; a useful negative result.

title: Expressed distress and portfolio risk in LLM investment advice
abstract: Does a client's expressed distress change chatbot investment advice? In a preregistered experiment, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GPT-6 Sol answered 5,040 structured allocation requests. In 4,320, three hypothetical investors described a loss, an upcoming withdrawal, or both, in neutral or distressed words over identical financial facts. After a loss, every request restated an unchanged risk tolerance. Distress cut the share of allocations above a stock–bond volatility reference matched to stated tolerance from 12.2% to 2.8% (-9.4 percentage points; 97.5% CI: -11.1 to -7.7), beyond the preregistered ±5-point equivalence band. The direction holds under alternative thresholds and covariances, although the decrease shrinks to 2.4–7.2 points. In an exploratory breakdown, the decrease came from the loss-only state (36.5% to 8.5%). All models accepted the task without asking for clarification. Coded retained-risk warnings ranged from 0.9% to 74.9% of explanations by the model. Whether warnings track risk within identical requests remains unresolved: two models barely varied their warnings, and the third model's descriptive interval admits both tracking and none. Two models warned more often when their allocations were supplied back unchanged than when they chose them. Taken together, expressed feeling changes the portfolio itself, not just the explanation.
why: Preregistered test of LLM advice under client distress; real financial task.

title: Multi-Asset Portfolio Selection with Machine Learning: Long-Run International Evidence
abstract: This study examines whether machine learning improves asset-class return forecasts, whether crosscountry information pooling further improves accuracy, and whether these gains also lead to better portfolio decisions. Using annual data for 16 countries covering equities, long-term bonds, bills, and housing from 1870 to 2020, we combine historical returns with macroeconomic and financial variables in a recursive forecasting framework. Pooled machine-learning forecasts significantly outperform both historical-mean forecasts and country-specific ML. These gains translate into higher Sharpe ratios for both international investors allocating across countries and domestic investors investing only within their home markets. Pooled ML also outperforms simple allocation rules such as equal weighting. The passive benchmark based on capital-weighted aggregate asset returns remains competitive in the baseline analysis, but pooled ML performs better when the universe is restricted to liquid asset classes or portfolio limits are relaxed. The results extend the machine-learning literature on long-run multi-asset allocation and highlight the value of pooling information across markets.
why: Pooled ML asset forecasts, Sharpe gains, long history; solid but familiar.

title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts A Controlled Study of Six Q8 Checkpoint Conversions
abstract: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from-0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.
why: Controlled LLM forecast probes; useful bias evidence but no trading outcome.

title: A Power Rule for Long-Dated Volatility When You Are in the Dark: Evidence from a 99-Stock Panel
abstract: Convertible bonds are three-to-five-year claims on equity volatility, yet the issuer often has no liquid long-dated options and only a short, noisy history. A one-parameter rule of thumb , maps an observed short-term volatility σ h into a long-term estimate σ i : it pulls very high observations down, pushes very low ones up and leaves the middle roughly alone. We test the rule out of sample on 99 listed stocks spanning eleven sectors and three size buckets, with histories of 20 to 52 years. Using a one-year volatility forecast as the input and the volatility realised over the following four years as the outcome, the median-fitted parameter is a = 0.61 (90% interval 0.55-0.65). This is stable across inputs and across threeto five-year horizons, and sits close to the practitioner prior a ≈ 0.7. The data are, if anything, more mean-reverting at the top of the range than the rule. We argue the shape follows from mean reversion in log volatility, and caution that the panel's survivorship biases the estimate toward too much reversion for high-volatility, weak-credit issuers-precisely the convertible universe. AI disclosure: an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used to run the experiments, write the code and draft the text; the idea and the rule are the author's own. * The views expressed are the author's own and do not necessarily represent those of Alken Asset Management.
why: Out-of-sample volatility rule on 99 stocks; clean, simple, forgettable.

title: From Algorithms to Agents: A Survey of LLM-Based Trading Systems
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now drive trading systems, from signal extractors to autonomous agents, but the literature is fragmented across markets, architectures, and evaluation practices. This survey traces the path from quantitative trading to LLM agents, organizes the literature by capability (perception, reasoning, action, memory, collaboration) and by six markets from equities to prediction markets, and maps 47 systems across both to show where evidence is thin. We audit evaluation protocols and consolidate head-to-head evidence against traditional quantitative baselines. Four findings emerge. First, the margins of independently rerun agents shrink or vanish, though the reruns cover few systems and many reported margins rest on windows of eight months or less, where an annualized Sharpe ratio has a standard error above one. Second, the best-supported hypothesis places the LLM upstream of the trade (text signals, factor and model code, and bounded execution tilts), although most upstream evidence comes from single author-run studies. Third, controlled comparisons do not establish a multi-agent advantage, though risk controls help where ablated. Fourth, structure and input design matter alongside the backbone, and the best structure depends on the backbone.
why: Survey of LLM trading, but its rerun-margin audit is useful evaluation evidence.

title: AI use and Risk Disclosure by Investment Advisers
abstract: Introduction: Investment advisers increasingly report using artificial intelligence (AI), but little is known about what they disclose about it in fiduciary filings. The SEC brought its first AI-washing enforcement actions in 2024, so regulators and researchers need a reproducible measure of AI disclosure. We provide largesample evidence on AI disclosure in Form ADV Part 2A brochures and show how the estimate depends on measurement design. Methods: We drew a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered investment advisers from a population of 16,223 firms, crossing adviser type (private-fund vs. wealth/retail) with 2024 assets-under-management (AUM) quartile. A large language model (LLM) classified the 388 available brochures under a prespecified five-label typology: investment-process use, operational or client-service use, AI-related risk, explicit non-use, and named AI vendors. We treated the LLM as a measurement instrument and validated it three ways: same-family reproducibility, blinded cross-family recoding of 180 brochures, and human verification of 158 cases. Secondary analyses compared brochures with 283 matched firm websites and applied a screen derived from SEC enforcement orders. Results: AI use is disclosed in 23.7% of brochures (22.7% survey-weighted), while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The within-brochure difference is significant (McNemar p = 0.036). Disclosure rises from 10.4% in the smallest AUM quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and is higher among private-fund advisers. Against human coding, the composite any-use measure achieves precision of 0.76 and sensitivity of 0.81. The same corpus yields estimates of 9.9%, 13.1%, and 23.7% under alternative constructs, adviser universes, and weighting schemes. A literal keyword rule misses or mislabels roughly a quarter of cases. A raw 17.3-percentage-point brochure-website gap disappears after conditioning on document length. None of the five enforcement-screen matches was adjudicated as an unsubstantiated promotional claim. Discussion: Advisers present AI at least as often as a risk as a capability, and disclosure is concentrated among larger and private-fund advisers. AI-disclosure prevalence reflects measurement design as much as adviser behavior, so estimates should be reported with their construct, universe, weighting, and validation. The validated framework and an open reproducibility capsule provide a baseline for monitoring AI claims and AI-washing in investment management.
why: LLM-based AI disclosure measurement; reproducible but narrow descriptive scope.

title: Predicting Financial Market Stress Regimes Using Multi-Asset Machine Learning
abstract: Early detection of systematic market stress remains a central challenge in quantitative finance, as traditional risk models often rely on lagging indicators that fail to capture sudden cross-asset panic. This paper introduces a cross-asset machine learning model classifying trading days into three distinct states (Low, Normal, and High Stress) using short-term momentum velocity, rolling volatility across equities, and fixed income. Using historical data from 2011 to 2025, we evaluate a non-linear Random Forest classifier against a linear Logistic Regression baseline across a strict chronological test/train split. The Random Forest Model achieved an out-of-sample accuracy of 59.21%, outperforming the Logistic Regression baseline by 18.52 percentage points. Our feature importance results demonstrate that equity momentum velocity acts as a critical leading indicator of market distress offering quantitative risk managers an earlier warning system before liquidity shock spreads to slower moving assets.
why: Stress classifier with a baseline, but no costs or trading implementation.

title: Navigating Without Hyperlinks: Internal Cross-References and Market Reactions
abstract: I examine the market relevance of the locating assistance firms provide through non-clickable internal crossreferences. Using Chinese A-share sustainability reports for FY2010-FY2025, I identify references to information needed to complete the current disclosure and measure how precisely they identify its location. For FY2010-FY2023, more precise guidance is associated with larger absolute market reactions, holding information-dependent reference density constant. This precision differential narrows across FY2022-FY2025, primarily reflecting a strengthening association for vague guidance while the estimated association for precise guidance remains approximately stable. This pattern is consistent with AI-assisted retrieval helping users complete the locating work left by broader cues. The findings show that non-clickable access is not a uniform information-acquisition environment and suggest that the relative value of firm-provided guidance depends on users' ability to complete the remaining search.
why: Chinese disclosure event study; AI is only a secondary interpretation.

title: New Forecasting Methods for an Old Problem: Predicting 147 Years of Systemic Financial Crises
abstract: This paper develops new forecasting methods for an old and ongoing problem by employing 13 machine learning algorithms to study 147 years of systemic financial crises across 17 countries. Findings suggest fixed capital formation is the most important variable. GDP per capita and consumer inflation have increased in prominence whereas debt-to-GDP, stock market and consumption were dominant at the turn of the 20 th century. A lag structure and rolling window both improve on optimised contemporaneous and individual country formats. Through a lag structure, banking sector predictors on average describe 28 percent of the variation in crisis prevalence, real sector 64 percent and external sector 8 percent. Nearly half of all algorithms reach peak performance through a lag structure. As measured through AUC, 𝐹 ! and Brier scores, top performing machine learning methods consistently produce high accuracy rates, with both random forests and gradient boosting in front with 77 percent correct forecasts, and consistently outperform traditional regression algorithms. Learning from other countries improve predictive strength, and non-linear models generally deliver higher accuracy rates than linear models. Algorithms retaining all variables perform better than those minimising the influence of variables.
why: Crisis prediction ML over long history; no trading or costs.

title: The transferable value of words: listing text improves spatial generalization of automated property valuation
abstract: Automated valuation models (AVMs) underpin decision support in mortgage lending, appraisal, and property platforms, yet they rely almost exclusively on structured attributes.We ask whether the unstructured text of listing advertisements carries pricing informationbeyond 35 structured attributes, using 2.9 million residential listings from Istanbul (20242026), the rst large-scale study of Turkish real-estate text. We benchmark gradient-boostingvaluation models in an ablation design: structured attributes only (M1), adding TFIDFterms (M2), adding GloVe document embeddings (M3), and both (M4), under random crossvalidation and a leave-county-out protocol that simulates deployment in previously unseen locations. In-sample, text contributes marginally (RMSE -0.5%), as location xed eectsabsorb most textual signal. In unseen counties, however, text-augmented models reduceRMSE by 3.610.8% in all held-out counties, showing that text is the transferable componentof the model: it substitutes for missing spatial knowledge where structured locationfeatures cannot generalize. These gains survive the exclusion of agency template text, whichis shown to account for most of the in-sample gain. SHAP analysis identies interpretableTurkish price-moving terms (view, deed status, credit eligibility, urgency, and luxury vocabulary) consistent with hedonic theory. We contribute a reproducible pipeline includingnear-duplicate detection (6.0% of ads are re-listings) and agency-template agging (9.0%),and release code and dictionaries.
why: Real-estate text valuation with spatial holdout; not financial markets.

title: Asymmetric Effects of Managerial Tone and Institutional Investor Behavior: Reconciling Limited Attention and Contrarian Investing
abstract: Abstract: Using annual reports of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2013 to 2024, this paper examines how managerial tone in the Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) shapes institutional investor behavior. We adopt an AI-based textual analysis approach that combines TF-IDF with a Support Vector Machine classifier, and decompose MD&A tone into a fundamental component and a net component. We find that net positive tone has a U-shaped relationship with institutional shareholdings, while net negative tone is positively associated with institutional shareholdings. The asymmetric effects of the two net tones produce a negative association between net overall tone and institutional shareholdings. Higher information transparency and industry competition strengthen this asymmetry, while financing constraints attenuate it. Our findings reconcile the competing predictions of limited attention and contrarian investing theories on how sophisticated investors process soft information, and offer practical implications for improving disclosure quality and refining disclosure rules.
why: Chinese MD&A tone via TF-IDF SVM; single-market, no trading result.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Financial technology (Fintech) innovation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), which has emerged as a disruptive technology across several industries, has had a substantial influence on the financial industry, notably financial technology (fintech). This abstract investigates how AI-powered solutions are revolutionising many sectors of financial services, as well as the significance of AI in fintech.. Artificial intelligence could potentially be used by fintech organisations to further enhance relationships with customers, increase effectiveness in operations, and stimulate innovation. Predictive analytics and machine learning algorithms are used to assess enormous quantities of data in order to provide helpful insights for risk assessment, fraud detection, and personalised financial advise. Chatbot and natural language processing (NLP) technologies are enabling intelligent virtual assistants that can engage with clients, answer questions, and give personalised support. This boosts client involvement and support. Furthermore, AI-powered algorithms are being utilised for algorithmic trading and investment management, allowing portfolio optimisation and decision-making to be automated. Robo-advisors, which are driven by AI, are gaining popularity because they provide personalised, low-cost investing advice to individual clients. Moreover, artificial intelligence has a tremendous influence on increasing fintech security and fraud prevention. AI-based solutions that detect suspicious trends, identify abnormalities, and warn potentially fraudulent activity in real time help to improve overall cybersecurity. Also, artificial intelligence has a knack to augment lending operations and credit assessment computations. Fintech businesses may effectively assess creditworthiness and offer loans to disadvantaged people with no traditional credit history by using alternative data sources and AI algorithms. Finally, AI has been producing more secure, individualised, and effective solutions, changing the public's perspective of fintech, and revolutionising financial services. Fintech businesses that use AI technology can gain a competitive advantage and foster innovation in the financial sector. However, it is crucial to remove the obstacles to AI's acceptability in order to assure its suitable and ethical deployment in the financial ecosystem.
why: Generic AI-in-fintech overview with no method, data, or evidence.

title: Diaspora Finance, Slow Microequity, and Artificial Intelligence: Channeling Transnational Patient Capital into Sustainable African Entrepreneurship
abstract: Financial inclusion and sustainable entrepreneurial development across Sub-Saharan Africa face an enduring structural dilemma: while regenerative entrepreneurship (notably in smallholder agriculture, agro-processing, local crafts, and ecological transitions) requires patient capital, risk protection, and relational support, prevailing digital credit models prioritize rapid loan turnover and high transaction velocity. Concurrently, although annual remittance inflows exceed $50 billion, diaspora capital remains overwhelmingly channeled into immediate consumption rather than productive enterprise equity due to cross-border information asymmetries and weak monitoring architectures. This paper examines how diaspora finance and Slow Finance microequity offer essential institutional alternatives to debt-driven microcredit, drawing conceptual foundations from Woody Tasch’s Slow Money movement, the seven-point taxonomy of grassroots fiduciary capital (Jayashankar, Ashta, & Rasmussen, 2015), civic solidarity investing (such as the French CIGALES), and transnational diaspora investment literature. Against this backdrop, we analyze how artificial intelligence (AI) and programmable rails can resolve the historical operational bottlenecks of diaspora micro-investing without imposing extractive velocity on local ventures. While initial coin offerings (ICOs) demonstrated that digital tokens can finance firm-level projects, their widespread governance failures highlight the danger of purely speculative, unanchored tokenization. We demonstrate that AI cannot alter the inherently slow, biological pace of sustainable agricultural enterprise; its legitimate developmental value lies in accelerating due diligence, verifying alternative ledgers, and automating cross-border revenue splits. We conclude that by linking digital payment rails to automated revenue-split smart contracts and decentralized oracles, hybrid intelligence can transform transnational remittances into patient, community-anchored equity for unincorporated sustainable enterprises.
why: Conceptual diaspora finance essay; AI is framing, not contribution.

title: Forensic Auditing in the Age of Synthetic Media: Frameworks for Detecting Deepfake-Generated Financial Fraud and Identity Spoofing (A Study of Selected Listed Financial Banks in Nigeria) Ujah, Iheanyichikwu Promise
abstract: The rapid convergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and sophisticated cybercrime has birthed a novel risk frontier: synthetic media fraud. Deepfake voice cloning, hyper-realistic executive video synthesis, and algorithmic identity spoofing severely threat the integrity of enterprise financial workflows and traditional forensic auditing mechanisms. This paper investigates the vulnerability of listed commercial banks in Nigeria to synthetic media fraud and formulates a robust mitigation architecture known as the Integrated Forensic-Media Audit (IFMA) Model. Adopting a Design Science Research (DSR) approach combined with empirical survey data from 180 senior forensic auditors, IT risk managers, and compliance officers across five systematically selected tier-1 listed banks (Access Bank, Zenith Bank, Guaranty Trust Bank, United Bank for Africa, and First Bank of Nigeria), this study evaluates the diagnostic efficacy of the IFMA model. Empirical analysis utilizing Descriptive Statistics, Pearson Correlation, and Multiple Linear Regression demonstrates that pre-audit technical verification, transactionalbehavioral triangulation, and zero-trust protocol integration exert a statistically significant positive effect on synthetic fraud detection efficiency (R² = 0.742, F = 168.45, p
why: Nigerian bank forensic survey; design-science, no transferable method.

title: Methane First: Sequencing Decarbonization Investment in the AI Data Center Boom
abstract: Data center development is caught between hyperscale demand driving trillions in capital spending [8, 22, 32] and growing local resistance over grid strain, water, land, and emissions [10, 20, 25]. Off-grid natural gas is becoming this buildout's transient bridge fuel, and reporting folds its methane and CO 2 into one number using a 100-year metric [15]. Methane warms hard and fades within decades while CO 2 does not, so the metric's time window could change which decarbonization investment looks better. We test this as a scenario analysis on 69 U.S. data centers with on-site gas turbines (many still proposed), in a scenario where the fleet grows to 350 by 2035: how should a fixed annual budget be split between methane leak repair (LDAR) and carbon capture (CCS)? Phase A treats LDAR as a one-time purchase, Phase B as a cost paid every year. We find the exact optimum (by dynamic programming (DP) in Phase B, by a direct argument in Phase A), train a reinforcement learning (RL) policy over 10 seeds, and test the cost assumptions with ablations. The optimal plan puts LDAR first under both GWP20 and GWP100 in both phases. Because the fleet-level problem is small enough to solve exactly, it also serves as a test of a model-free RL policy: using only a simulator of the fleet, RL recovers the exact optimum in 17 of 20 Phase B runs (the rest within 0.6%) and in every Phase A run. This is the check RL needs before it is used on richer versions of the problem (random leaks, uncertain build-out, per-facility budgets), where exact dynamic programming no longer scales. With other settings at baseline, the two metrics disagree only when re-buying leak repair each year costs 25-60% of its one-time cost while capture is a lasting purchase, which a closed-form break-even horizon explains. Symmetric costs, finite capture life, and falling capture costs all keep LDAR first. Avoided-emission totals are scenario outputs, not forecasts.
why: Methane and data center capex scenario analysis; not finance ML.

title: Predictive Modeling for Corporate Insolvency: An Algorithmic Approach to Financial Risk
abstract: Corporate bankruptcy poses a significant threat to economic stability, occurring when an enterprise is unable to meet its debt obligations and requires creditor intervention. This study employs machine learning techniques to predict the likelihood of corporate insolvency based on key financial indicators. To forecast bankruptcy, we evaluated multiple models: Support Vector Machines (SVM), XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Decision Trees. Our empirical results indicate that Random Forest is the most effective predictive technique, achieving a training accuracy of 99.1%. Furthermore, we implemented several deep learning architectures-specifically Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN)-for comparative analysis. These deep learning models yielded highly competitive training accuracies of approximately 98%. Ultimately, this research not only improves upon traditional econometric forecasting models but also establishes a robust machine learning framework for predicting financial distress.
why: Bankruptcy classifiers reporting 99% training accuracy; weak evaluation.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Labor Market Monopsony: A Nonlinear Analysis
abstract: Based on data from Chinese listed firms from 2007 to 2024, this study empirically examines the nonlinear impact of AI penetration on labor market monopsony power. The results reveal a significant U-shaped relationship: in the early stage, AI enhances productivity and broadens workers’ external employment options, weakening monopsony power; beyond a threshold, automation substitutes for routine tasks, narrows options, and strengthens monopsony power. This effect is more pronounced in non-financial, private, and labor-intensive firms. Increased AI investment flattens the U-curve and shifts the inflection point to the right. This study offers micro-level evidence on structural shifts in labor market power during digital transformation.
why: AI and labor monopsony in China; not finance ML.

title: Perceived Transaction Security and Consumer Trust in AI-supported Mastercard Payments in Bangladesh
abstract: Digital payment ecosystems increasingly combine card networks, mobile interfaces, automated fraud controls, authentication technologies, and artificial-intelligence-supported risk monitoring. In such environments, perceived transaction security is not only a technical attribute but also a trust-building signal. This study examines whether consumers' perceived transaction security is associated with trust in Mastercard-enabled payments in Bangladesh and whether trust functions as a mechanism linking security perceptions to cashless-payment intention. The study uses a quantitative, cross-sectional survey of adult consumers in Bangladesh with relevant Mastercard or Mastercard-enabled payment experience, using a five-point Likert instrument and a theory-driven structural model informed by Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) and trust theory. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 cases are fully populated and were retained for analysis; the remaining 15 rows are blank placeholders. All 385 retained cases passed the embedded attention check. Because the documented questionnaire operationalises transaction security and trust but does not provide validated AI-specific construct wording, AI is treated as an ecosystem context rather than as a causal latent variable. A reproducible variance-oriented analysis was conducted using construct scores, bootstrap inference, mediation analysis, measurement diagnostics, multicollinearity assessment, and 10-fold out-of-sample prediction. why: Consumer survey on payment trust; no quantitative finance contribution.

title: Mechano-Allosteric Catch-Bond & Visco-Elastic Null-space Watermarks (MAC-VENPW): Zero-retraining Provenance, Eshelby Splice Forensics, and Radioactive Distillation Defense for Frozen LLMs
abstract: The Fundamental Doubt & Conceptual Breakthrough: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) encompass 10 10 to 10 12 parameters trained over trillions of tokens, making full-network retraining or architectural surgery to embed cryptographic provenance watermarks computationally and thermodynamically impossible. A natural engineering intuition is to freeze 100% of the pretrained LLM backbone and attach a lightweight, fixed-weight watermark block at the output head. However, our first-principles mathematical and empirical audit reveals that both naive fixed-weight blocks and state-of-the-art token-level watermarks (Kirchenbauer et al., ICML, 2023; Kuditipudi et al., TMLR, 2024) suffer from four fundamental failure modes: (1) The Intra-Formula Symbolic Corruption Trap, where constant logit shifts (δ = 2.0) or even memoryless entropy gates corrupt deterministic numbers, biomechanical units, and transitional variable tokens inside multi-step partial differential equations (27.1% numerical error and +34.2% perplexity inflation for a naive fixed block; 3.3% intra-formula corruption for memoryless entropy gating); (2) Phase Shattering Under Paraphrase & Indels, where sliding-window n-gram hashes lose synchronization (5.8% true positive rate under a 30% edit attack); (3) Vulnerability to Spoofing/Splicing & Open-Weight Stripping, where adversaries either delete an external wrapper module or splice human-written paragraphs into watermarked documents; and (4) Severe False-Positive Bias Against Non-Native (ESL) Human Writers (85.7% false-positive rate for post-hoc perplexity detectors; Liang et al., Patterns, 2023). Here, we originate from an unexplored biophysical question: why do artificial neural networks treat logit perturbations as memoryless algebraic shifts, whereas living cytoskeletal proteins such as talin and extracellular matrix hydrogels use fractional viscoelastic stress memory and force-gated catch-bonds to protect structural integrity while transmitting mechanical information? We invent the Mechano-Allosteric Catch-Bond & Visco-Elastic Null-Space Phase-Locking Watermark (MAC-VENPW). MAC-VENPW models the frozen LLM's probability simplex as a Fractional Caputo-Zener Viscoelastic Continuum coupled to M = 4 talin-inspired Cryptic Orthogonal Subspace Bundles (R3, R8, R10, R12) embedded inside the zero-sum synonym null-space of the frozen unembedding matrix W U. Across N = 1, 200 passages, MAC-VENPW achieves 100.0% exact numerical and PDE formula fidelity, restricts perplexity drift to +0.80%, sustains 99.33% TPR (Z = 12.73 ± 2.44, p = 3.73 × 10-149) under 30% paraphrase + indel attacks via 4-band Lomb-Scargle spectral demodulation, exhibits 0.0% ESL false-positive rate, localizes spliced human forgery spans via Eshelby's Configurational Stress Tensor (IoU = 0.942), embeds a 64-bit Walsh-Hadamard payload (99.41% bit accuracy), survives student knowledge distillation (Z radioactive = 8.94 at 25% teacher data), and folds algebraically into W U (D KS = 0.0781, p = 0.832) with zero extra inference FLOPs.
why: LLM watermarking; off-topic for financial research.
